rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Collisions divide by what survives. **Momentum is always conserved** in an isolated collision; **kinetic energy only in elastic ones**. Elastic collisions (billiard balls, gas molecules) obey $v_1 = \frac{(m_1-m_2)u_1 + 2m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2}$ — with equal masses the velocities simply exchange, a light projectile rebounds off a heavy target, and a heavy one ploughs through sending the light target off at nearly double…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Elastic: v₁ = [(m₁−m₂)u₁ + 2m₂u₂]/(m₁+m₂); v₂ = [(m₁−m₂)u₂ + 2m₁u₁]/(m₁+m₂) - u₂ = 0: v₁ = (m₁−m₂)u₁/(m₁+m₂); v₂ = 2m₁u₁/(m₁+m₂) - Perfectly inelastic: v = (m₁u₁+m₂u₂)/(m₁+m₂) - KE lost = KE_i − KE_f

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Momentum vs KE conservation:** momentum survives every isolated collision; KE survives only elastic ones — the lost KE becomes heat and deformation.  ·  **Elastic vs 'bouncy':** a real bouncy ball's collision is inelastic (it rebounds lower); only idealised collisions are elastic.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the objects do NOT lose ALL their kinetic energy — only the KE relative to the center of mass can be lost.  ·  The coefficient of restitution e depends on the materials, not on the velocities of the colliding bodies.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Bullet in block*** — 0.02 kg at 500 m/s into 4.98 kg: v = 2 m/s, 2490 J lost (NEB 2022).

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Verified PYQs: elastic vs inelastic difference (2020, 3m); bullet-block numerical (2022, 4m).

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Solve 5 one-dimensional elastic collision problems using the standard formulas.  ·  Solve 5 perfectly inelastic collision problems finding the common velocity and KE loss.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Sticking → common velocity = total p / total m."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (4m): A 2 kg ball at 6 m/s collides elastically head-on with a 2 kg ball at rest. Find the final velocities.** — Equal masses exchange velocities: the first stops (v₁ = 0), the second moves off at 6 m/s. Momentum (12 kg·m/s) and KE (36 J) both conserved.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Most-tested: the difference question (2020) and embedding numerical (2022). Learn the three special cases of the elastic formulas.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Equal masses exchange velocities:** the elastic-collision signature — and the reason hydrogen moderates neutrons in reactors.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: All collisions conserve momentum; only elastic ones conserve KE.  ·  Elastic (u₂ = 0): v₁ = (m₁−m₂)u₁/(m₁+m₂); v₂ = 2m₁u₁/(m₁+m₂); equal masses exchange velocities.  ·  Perfectly inelastic: v = (m₁u₁+m₂u₂)/(m₁+m₂); maximum KE loss.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Gas molecules collide almost perfectly elastically — without that, the kinetic theory's pressure predictions would fail.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s hits a stationary 2 kg ball in an elastic collision. The final velocity of the first ball is: → A  ·  A 3 kg ball moving at 4 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg ball in a perfectly inelastic collision. Their common velocity is: → A

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — What Survives a Crash Every collision conserves momentum; only some conserve kinetic energy. The classification — elastic, inelastic, perfectly inelastic — decides how the bodies separate, and powers billiards, crash engineering and particle detectors.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2020) | Type | Momentum | Kinetic energy | Separation | Example | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Elastic** | Conserved | Conserved | Bodies separate | Billiard balls, gas molecules, atomic collisions | | **Inelastic** | Conserved | Partly lost (heat, sound, deformation) | Bodies separate | Most real collisions; a dropped ball that bounces lower | |…  ·  ## 3. Conceptual Relationships - **To Topics 11–12:** momentum conservation is the universal collision law; this topic adds the energy bookkeeping. - **To Topic 20:** lost KE becomes heat — non-conservative dissipation inside the collision. - **To Kinetic Theory (Unit 13):** gas molecules collide elastically — the model's foundation.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: In an elastic collision between equal masses where one is initially at rest, the masses exchange velocities.  ·  Momentum is conserved in ALL collisions (elastic and inelastic) as long as no external force acts.  ·  NEB collision problems: always check whether the collision is elastic (use both conservation laws) or inelastic (use only momentum conservation).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: "Momentum always balances; kinetic energy only sometimes."  ·  Why does a neutron slow down fastest colliding with hydrogen?  ·  Solve 3 equal-mass elastic collision problems using the velocity-exchange shortcut.
